title: Satisfaction
hook: Anselm pictured the cross as Christ restoring God's honor on our behalf

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christus Victor: a broken gate, and death that swallowed life and couldn't keep it down. Your line was death is defeated. What fear did you taunt? Day one thousand eighty-three.

"Forgive us our debts." That's how the Lord's Prayer reads in Matthew's Gospel, in the old King James words. Not mistakes. Not trespasses. Debts. As if every wrong leaves an unpaid bill behind it. Anselm, the archbishop who asked why God became human, took that picture very seriously. Some historians link his thinking to a world of lords and oaths, where honor was owed, and a broken promise had to be made good. And he asked a hard, clear question. If sin is a debt to God, what does it take to settle it? Yesterday's picture was a battlefield. Today's is a ledger. Today's word: satisfaction.

Forget the modern meaning, the feeling after a good meal. In Anselm's picture, satisfaction means making amends: doing what's needed to put a wrong right. Here's how he lays it out, in his dialogue Why God Became Human. Every creature owes God honor: its whole life, its whole will, turned toward God. Sin is refusing that. It's holding back what was owed. And here's the trap. Even if you lived perfectly from tomorrow on, you'd only be paying what you already owed for tomorrow. Nothing is left over to cover yesterday. So the debt stands. Anselm says there are only two ways a wrong against honor can end: either it's made good, or it's punished. God, he says, chooses to make it good. Not a penalty, but a repair. On day one thousand eighty we heard who Anselm thought could do that: only one who is both God and human. Christ's freely given life, which he never owed to death, is a gift so great it more than covers what humanity held back. Paul has his own picture of a bill wiped out: "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross." Not every church tells the story with Anselm's ledger, and those who do build on it in different ways. Notice one thing it is not. In Anselm's telling, the cross isn't punishment. It's payment. That difference comes up again tomorrow.

Here's the practice: think of a debt someone paid for you. Settle, and breathe. It doesn't have to be money. Someone covered for you. Someone made good on a promise you broke. Someone stayed up so you could sleep. Let one picture come. Notice the size of it, and that you couldn't have paid it yourself. If you pray, you can hold that picture next to the cross and say thank you. If you don't, just stay with the person who paid. The bell holds the time.
Satisfaction. In Anselm's picture, making amends for a wrong against God's honor: a debt humans owe and only the God-man can pay.
Your line: he paid what we owed. Today, quietly pay one small thing forward for someone who won't know it was you. Day one thousand eighty-three.

howItsDone: Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's wording ask God to forgive their debts, and in some churches the language of Christ paying what humanity owed is heard in hymns, sermons and the prayers at communion.

pairs: the handwriting nailed to the cross

myth: in Anselm's picture, the cross is a punishment
Anselm says a wrong is either made good or punished. God chooses to make it good: payment, not punishment.
Matthew's Lord's Prayer in the King James asks God to forgive our debts
"forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
Anselm thought good behavior from now on could pay for the past
you'd only be paying what you already owed for the future. nothing is left over for yesterday.

fork.setup: you're Anselm. honor owed to God has been held back. how can the wrong end?
options: God simply lets it go, as if it never happened.
it must be either made good or punished, and God chooses to make it good.
humans try harder until the debt is cleared.
fork.reveal: Anselm says it's satisfaction or punishment. God chooses satisfaction, and only someone both human and divine can pay it.

original.note: Latin: Anselm's word for making amends, putting a wrong right.

trapdoor: what you thought: satisfaction means feeling pleased.
what it means: in Anselm's picture, making amends. humans owe God honor they held back, and the God-man pays it.
what a scholar hears: Anselm's either-or. a wrong ends in satisfaction or punishment, and he puts the cross on the satisfaction side.
recall: each person dwelling in the others
